statement: Jack Garman's handwritten list of program alarms (often cited as the basis for the 1202/1201 Go calls) could not be confirmed in any retrieved primary source.

statement: An ALSJ contributor relays Gene Kranz's account that the final pre-mission landing simulation (with Dave Scott and Jim Irwin in the LM simulator) was aborted unnecessarily by Mission Control because of a 1201 program alarm.

notes: ALSJ editorial/contributor commentary (retrospective secondary analysis, not a contemporaneous record). Second-hand relay of Kranz's book 'Failure is Not an Option' (not retrieved). Treat the simulation as reported, not independently verified.

statement: The Mission Report anomaly analysis states five computer program alarms occurred during descent before low gate and that guidance and control performance was not affected.
locator: Section 16.2.5 Computer Alarms During Descent, p. 16-12
excerpt: Five computer program alarms occurred during descent prior to the low-gate phase of the trajectory. The performance of guidance and control functions was not affected.
notes: Excerpt transcribed from the OCR text layer of the scanned report; OCR letter-spacing artifacts normalized, wording unchanged.

statement: The alarms were of the Executive overflow type and indicated that more than 10 percent of computational capacity was preempted by unexpected counter interrupts from the coupling data units interfacing with the rendezvous radar shaft and trunnion resolvers.
excerpt: The alarms indicated that more than 10 percent of the computational capacity of the computer was preempted by unexpected counter interrupts of the type generated by the coupling data units that interface with the rendezvous radar shaft and trunnion resolvers
notes: Excerpt transcribed from the OCR text layer of the scanned report; OCR letter-spacing artifacts normalized, wording unchanged.

statement: The Executive schedules repetitive jobs such as Servicer (every 2 seconds) open-loop; if a job is slowed by counter interrupts it schedules the same job again and reserves another storage area; when all are assigned a program alarm and software restart result. Multiple scheduling of the same job produced the alarms.
excerpt: A review of the jobs that can run during descent leads to the conclusion that multiple scheduling of the same job produced the program alarms.
notes: Excerpt transcribed from the OCR text layer of the scanned report; OCR letter-spacing artifacts normalized, wording unchanged.

statement: Analyses and simulations identified the cause of the multiple job scheduling as primarily counter interrupts from the rendezvous radar coupling data unit.
excerpt: The cause for the multiple scheduling of jobs has been identified by analyses and simulations to be primarily counter interrupts from the rendezvous radar coupling data unit.
notes: Excerpt transcribed from the OCR text layer of the scanned report; OCR letter-spacing artifacts normalized, wording unchanged.

statement: With the rendezvous radar mode switch in AUTO or SLEW, resolver excitation came from the ATCA 28-volt 800-hertz supply, which was frequency-locked but not phase-locked to the PGNS 800-hertz reference; phase/amplitude differences made the CDUs slew digitally and send continuous pulses to the computer.
excerpt: The attitude and translation control assembly voltage is locked in frequency with the primary guidance and navigation system voltage through the system's control of the PCM and timing electronics frequency, but it is not locked in phase.
notes: Excerpt transcribed from the OCR text layer of the scanned report; OCR letter-spacing artifacts normalized, wording unchanged. Physical mechanism as officially documented.

statement: The Mission Report quantifies the load: maximum 6.4 kpps per CDU, 11.7 microseconds each; 12.8 kpps from two radar CDUs would take 15 percent of computer time, while the computer normally runs at about 90 percent of capacity during peak powered-descent activity.
excerpt: If a maximum of 12.8 kpps are received (two radar coupling data units), 15 percent of the available computer time will be spent in processing the radar interrupts.
notes: Excerpt transcribed from the OCR text layer of the scanned report; OCR letter-spacing artifacts normalized, wording unchanged.

statement: When capacity is exceeded, some repetitively scheduled routines are not completed before the next computation cycle; the computer then generates a software restart and displays an Executive overflow alarm.
excerpt: When the capacity of the computer is exceeded, some repetitively scheduled routines will not be completed prior to the start of the next computation cycle.
notes: Excerpt transcribed from the OCR text layer of the scanned report; OCR letter-spacing artifacts normalized, wording unchanged.

statement: The Mission Report's descent section states the alarms did not degrade any primary guidance or control function but did interfere with the crew's early assessment of the landing approach.

notes: Excerpt transcribed from the OCR text layer of the scanned report; OCR letter-spacing artifacts normalized, wording unchanged.

statement: Eyles states the problem stole approximately 13% of the computer's duty cycle and caused five program alarms and software restarts.
excerpt: An uncorrected problem in the rendezvous radar  interface stole approximately 13% of the computer's duty cycle, resulting in five program alarms and software restarts.
notes: Retrospective participant account (2004), secondary. Double space after 'radar' is in the source.

statement: Eyles states the duty-cycle margin was over 15% before landing-radar acquisition, about 13% after, and 10% or less with a Verb 16 Noun 68 monitor display, so a ~13% drain exceeded available time.
excerpt: With a 10% margin and a 13% drain, the LGC simply did not have enough CPU time to perform all the functions that were required.
notes: Retrospective participant analysis; consistent with Aldrin's real-time 16/68 correlation (A11-C019).

statement: Eyles describes restart protection, motivated by possible hardware glitches, as having shed computational load (flushing stale SERVICER jobs and terminating non-restart-protected functions such as the Verb 16 Noun 68 monitor).
excerpt: Here a system of restart protection that was primarily motivated by the possibility of hardware glitches synergistically provided a means to shed computational load in response to a software logjam caused by TLOSS.
notes: Retrospective participant account; safeguard mechanism.

statement: Eyles states that in P64 the essential software alone left less than a 10% margin, so restarts flushed the queue but could not shed load; Armstrong's switch to ATT HOLD and then P66 eased the burden and no alarms occurred in P66.
excerpt: After 2 minutes and 20 seconds spent maneuvering in P66 without alarms, the LM landed.
notes: Retrospective participant analysis; the Mission Report's Table 5-I shows no alarms after 102:42:58 (P66 entered 102:43:22), consistent.

statement: CONTRADICTION (alarm timing): ALSJ commentary says Mission Report Table 5-I gives the 1201 alarm at 102:41:32, but Table 5-I lists 102:41:32 as 'Enter program P64' and the 1201 alarm at 102:42:18; ALSJ likewise cites 102:39:02 for the first 1202 although the table's first 1202 is 102:38:22.

statement: CONTRADICTION (computational drain): the Mission Report says more than 10 percent of capacity was preempted and computes 15 percent at the 12.8 kpps maximum; Eyles gives approximately 13% (Grumman worst-case 13.36%); Martin recalls the computer seemed to run at 80% of normal speed.

notes: Other sides: A11-S01 sec. 16.2.5 (A11-C029, A11-C033) and A11-S20 (A11-C044, A11-C045; Grumman 13.36% per Eyles). The figures are broadly compatible (10-15%) but not identical; Martin's 80% is a real-time impression.

statement: CONTRADICTION (which jobs overflowed): Adler states repeated jobs to process (non-existent) rendezvous radar data were scheduled, whereas the Mission Report and Eyles state the counter interrupts slowed the regular jobs (Servicer) so the same job was re-scheduled.

notes: Other side: A11-S01 sec. 16.2.5 (A11-C030, A11-C031); Eyles A11-S20 SERVICER explanation. Adler wrote 'as I recall'; the official mechanism is preferred.

statement: CONTRADICTION (blame framing): Martin's recollection frames the cause as the crew setting the switch to AUTO per their procedures book; Eyles calls the 'checklist error' formulation inaccurate and blames an ICD; Armstrong said the configuration had been agreed and used in all simulations; the Mission Report attributes it to the interface configuration.

notes: Other sides: A11-S21 (A11-C042), A11-S16 (A11-C037), A11-S01 (A11-C032, A11-C036). Also: Martin says AUTO, Aldrin/Armstrong say Slew during descent - the Mission Report covers both (AUTO or SLEW).

statement: CONTRADICTION (timing of the ascent fix): Martin recalls the Flight Director's switch instruction as the last message just before ascent ignition, and Eyles says George Silver reached MIT representatives in Houston less than one hour before lift-off; the transcript shows the RR-off checklist change passed at 121:41:37, about 2 h 40 min before lift-off at 124:22:00.8.

notes: Other sides: A11-S09 GET 121:41:37 (A11-C082); A11-S01 sec. 13.1 (A11-C081); Eyles A11-S20 ('on the morning of July 21, less than one hour before lunar liftoff'). No such instruction near 124:22 was found in the ALSJ ascent transcript; real-time record preferred. 'Glenn Lunney' as spelled in source.
